newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore opposition member to fight court orders.
newsitem.headline: Singapore opposition member to fight court orders.

text.p: An opposition politician who lost a dozen libel cases to the Singapore leadership that could cost him millions said on Tuesday that he would fight back.

Tang Liang Hong, an unsuccessful candidate in January elections, told Reuters he would appeal certain court orders that led up to Monday's verdict, which found him guilty of libeling Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and other ruling party members during the election campaign.
Tang, who fled the country after the poll, said if he succeeded in an appeal against the orders, then the judgement would collapse.

Among the orders he said he intended to challenge was one that told him to list all his assets in an affidavit and set aside those worth $Singapore $11.2 million (US$7.8 million) to cover damages and costs if found guilty.

"If I can set aside ... the order of court against me for filing the affidavit of assets, which is oppressive, then the entire judgement signed by the plaintiffs against me will fall because they are based on (the) order of court," Tang said in a telephone interview.
Tang told Reuters that he was in Malaysia. He has not returned to Singapore since he left after the election, saying that he feared for his life.
Tang stood unsuccessfully for the Worker's Party in the January 2 general election in which the PAP won 81 of parliament's 83 seats.
In a rare night sitting on Monday, the Singapore High Court ruled that libel suits against Tang brought by Goh and 11 other senior members of the PAP succeeded because Tang presented no defence.
Tang's lawyer, Workers' Party leader Joshua Jayeretnam, said on Monday he wanted to withdraw from the cases.

Jeyaretnam said he had received no instructions from Tang and so could not argue for him. Lawyers for Goh and the PAP leaders charged this was a delaying tactic and urged the court to pronounce judgement.
It did so, saying Tang had presented no defence to the dozen cases stemming from the election campaign.
Goh charged that Tang, who stood in the hardest-fought constituency, was a "Chinese chauvinist" who endangered racial harmony in Singapore, where ethnic Chinese are in the majority.
Singapore has substantial minorities of Malays and Indians, and English is the working language to avert potential friction.
Tang accused Goh and other PAP leaders who repeated the chauvinism charge of lying. They promptly sued him for libel.
Tang, a lawyer, did not turn up on Tuesday for a hearing of a 13th case stemming from the elections.
The case was brought by Goh after Tang had told reporters from London that he feared arrest if he returned to Signapore to defend himself.
Goh promised no such thing would happen, then hit Tang with another libel suit when the Workers' Party man asked publicly why he should trust the prime minister.
The next hearing in the case is set for Friday and Tang suggested he was in no hurry to return to defend himself, even though, as on Monday, he risked losing the case by not turning up.
"Why is it so essential for me to come back?" he asked. "What is the hurry?"
